item.title: The use of AI chatbot on efl students’ speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate: through the lens of activity theory
item.description:
BMC Psychology
English as a foreign language (EFL) educators have increasingly incorporated Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language learning; accordingly, this study explored the role of an AI-supported speaking tool in speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate (WTC) among Chinese EFL students. Activity theory refers to a proper and applicable structure proposed for investigating how AI chatbots affect different dimensions. Applying this theory to the research allows for analyzing the complicated interactions between those factors and a comprehension of the effect of AI chatbots (EAP Talk) on learners’ WTC, speaking proficiency, and speaking anxiety. A total of 113 participants were initially recruited (58 EG, 55 CG); after excluding four multivariate outliers (all from the EG), the primary analytic sample comprised 109 learners (54 EG, 55 CG). Full-sample results ( N = 113) are also reported and were consistent in direction, though smaller in magnitude for speaking anxiety (see Sensitivity Analysis). Using pretests, the participants’ levels of speaking abilities, anxiety, and WTC were assessed prior to the intervention. Subsequently, the EG received AI-supported speaking practice through EAP Talk, an AI-based speaking assessment and feedback application that facilitated iterative practice and immediate automated feedback, whereas the CG was taught the same material without the use of this tool. Using post-tests following the treatment, both groups were evaluated on their speaking skills, anxiety, and WTC. The results revealed notable posttest differences between the two groups: WTC showed a medium effect size, speaking anxiety showed a large effect size, and speaking skill showed a very large effect size. Overall, the results suggest that the EAP Talk intervention was associated with improved speaking performance and WTC, as well as reduced speaking anxiety among the participating EFL students. Interpreting the findings through the lens of Activity Theory helps situate the results within the broader relationships among learners, tools, and instructional context; however, the theory is used here as an interpretive lens rather than as a directly tested explanatory model.

item.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
item.description:
Journal of Educational Computing Research
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.

item.title: How does community of inquiry matter? Mediating effects and configurational pathways linking project-based learning design to learning engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has reshaped animation students’ skill profiles and the conditions of instructional design in project-based learning (PBL) studios. We examine whether and how perceptions of PBL design are associated with Learning Engagement (LE), treating AIGC-assisted PBL studios as the research context rather than testing generative AI as a model variable. Drawing on Community of Inquiry (CoI) theory, we examine Problem Driven (PD), Project Design (PDe), Project Implementation (PI), and Project Evaluation (PE) as antecedents; Cognitive Presence (CP), Social Presence (SP), and Teaching Presence (TP) as statistical mediators; and LE as the outcome. We analyzed two-wave survey data from 490 upper-year animation students using PLS-SEM and fsQCA. PBL and CoI were measured concurrently at T1, and LE at T2; indirect effects therefore represent indirect statistical associations rather than mediation with a fully established temporal sequence. PD, PDe, and PI showed significant positive direct associations with LE. PE’s zero-order and single-predictor associations were positive, but its direct path coefficient became significantly negative after controlling for the other PBL dimensions and CoI mediators. The coefficient was sensitive to model specification, suggesting possible statistical suppression; it should not be interpreted as evidence that evaluation itself inherently inhibits engagement. The three CoI dimensions showed significant statistical mediation associations across all 12 indirect paths. TP and SP had relatively higher point estimates of indirect statistical associations, but differences between indirect effects were not formally tested; no dimension is claimed to be optimal. PE’s positive indirect associations through CoI partially offset its negative net direct association without reversing the total association after adjustment. The extent of this offset may depend on the degree to which CoI-related experiences are concurrently reported. fsQCA identified seven high-engagement configurations. No individual PBL dimension was indispensable. CoI dimensions appeared as core or peripheral conditions, although not every configuration included all three. These findings clarify the dual pathways linking evaluation and engagement through indirect statistical associations and configurational conditions, and provide guidance for optimizing PBL under different resource constraints. Conclusions are limited to AIGC-assisted PBL studios and do not establish the instructional effects of generative AI.

item.title: Psychological mechanisms of perceived technological dependence on generative artificial intelligence tools: perceived knowledge, trust, anxiety, and self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

item.title: Twenty-Five Years, Five Projects, and Five Reflections on Accessible Computing
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
I began working on accessible computing in 2001 at the start of my doctoral program by developing word prediction software for Palm PDA devices [4]. Today, 25 years later, accessibility has remained a core focus of my work and the work of my students in the field of human-computer interaction (HCI). In this keynote, I will share five projects that have significantly shaped my work, along with five reflections that continue to inform my perspective. My goal is to convey ideas from which I would have benefitted 25 years ago as a junior researcher starting in accessible computing. My five projects are EdgeWrite [9], Slide Rule [3], enhanced area cursors [1] and, in particular, the Pointing Magnifier [2], ability-based design [7,8], and the epidemiological model of mobile app accessibility [5,6]. My five reflections concern prioritizing depth, the power of participant-driven prototyping, the opportunities and obligations of field deployments, the importance of conceptual contributions, and the value of cross-disciplinary deep-dives. I conclude by addressing some of the promises and pitfalls of artificial intelligence for accessibility, drawing on these reflections to light our way.

item.title: Designing and Evaluating an AI-Powered Figma Plugin for Accessibility Education
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Digital accessibility barriers are easier to prevent during design than to remediate after implementation, yet accessibility is often taught and practiced as a downstream concern. Despite growing attention in computing and design education, accessibility efforts continue to emphasize code-level auditing, remediation, and compliance checking, with less attention to early design decisions. The shift-left principle seeks to address this gap by embedding accessibility from the initial UX design phase, but its adoption remains limited. To explore how AI can support this shift, we developed a Figma plugin that uses a multimodal large language model (LLM) to evaluate UI frames against WCAG criteria and provide contextual, design-stage feedback. In a three-week deployment, 89 practicing professionals and computing or design students used the plugin alongside existing tools (Stark and Axe for Designers) and reported their perceptions, experiences, and self-reported abilities through pre- and post-use surveys. Overall, 92.1% reported identifying accessibility issues earlier, 96.6% reported productivity gains, and participants rated recommendation likelihood (M=4.25/5) and generated specification accuracy (M=4.08/5) highly. Findings also suggest that contextual AI feedback can help learners identify and reason about accessibility issues earlier in the design process. We conclude with practical takeaways for integrating AI-supported tools into accessibility education.

item.title: Zeno: Improving the Fidelity and Pedagogical Value of LLM-Generated Alt Text with BLV-Informed Guidelines and Iterative Prompting
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generating pedagogically useful alternative text (alt text) for advanced computer science course materials requires more than describing visual appearance: blind and low-vision learners often need descriptions that support tracing, comparison, equation reading, and task completion. This work-in-progress study examines how blind-learner-informed guidance can improve LLM-generated alt text for an online AI course. Inspired by a blind student’s longitudinal course experience, we introduce Delta, a CS-specific guideline for task-operable alt text, and Zeno, an iterative LLM workflow that generates, critiques, and revises alt text against the source material. In a formative evaluation with two sighted reviewers and one blind reviewer, Delta-informed prompting and Zeno substantially outperformed a WCAG-only baseline in sighted fidelity, pass rate, and diagnostic error patterns. These findings suggest that blind-learner-informed guidance can improve the pedagogical usefulness of LLM-generated alt text for technical course materials.

item.title: Learning Python as a Blind Programmer in an AI-Mediated Environment: An Autoethnographic Study
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Programming education is increasingly mediated by AI tools, yet little is known about how blind learners—particularly non-native English speakers—integrate these tools into learning, or where AI fails to address accessibility barriers. This paper presents an eight-week autoethnographic study of a blind, Chinese-speaking doctoral student learning introductory Python through Khan Academy’s curriculum with screen readers, a Braille display, and AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini). Drawing on detailed learning diaries and human–AI interaction logs analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis, we examine how AI mediates accessibility, cognition, and language during programming learning. Findings show that AI simultaneously functions as an accessibility interpreter, cognitive scaffold, and linguistic mediator, yet also introduces epistemic uncertainty, accessibility hallucinations, inconsistent cross-lingual terminology, and clear limits with non-textual cues. We argue that AI reconfigures rather than solves accessibility, and derive design implications for AI-assisted programming tools prioritizing explicit code structure, screen-reader integration, calibrated trust, and terminology-aware multilingual support.

item.title: Towards Accessible AI Literacy: Investigating How Teachers of Blind and Low-Vision Students Integrate Generative AI in Pedagogical Practices
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools are reshaping the educational landscape; yet, how teachers working with blind and low vision (BLV) students integrate these tools into their pedagogical practices remains underexplored. To address this gap, we interviewed 17 teachers of BLV students to investigate how they leverage GenAI to fulfill their teaching responsibilities and educate BLV students about these tools. We found that teachers incorporated GenAI for personalized lesson planning and tasks specific to BLV education, while counteracting biases favoring sighted teaching methods. They addressed BLV students’ curiosity and concerns about GenAI and taught them prompt formulation strategies that support their access needs in academic and daily tasks, although occasionally perpetuating their own misconceptions about GenAI to students. They expressed concerns about students’ overreliance on GenAI lowering foundational accessibility-related skills. We discuss ways to promote accessible AI literacy and outline design considerations for incorporating GenAI to support teachers’ BLV-specific instructional responsibilities and for integrating GenAI responsibly in BLV education.

item.title: A Recipe for Access: Visually Oriented Recipe Instructions as an Accessibility Barrier for Blind and Low-Vision Cooks
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
For people who are blind or have low vision (BLV), barriers to independent cooking are associated with reduced dietary quality and elevated health risks. One such barrier is embedded in recipe language itself: phrases such as “cook until golden brown” or “sauté until translucent” require visual monitoring. That such phrases exist is not new; what has been missing is evidence of their scale and an account of what BLV cooks do in their place. We use the term Visually Oriented Instructional Descriptor (VizOID) for this kind of recipe language. Across 573,986 recipes and 3.85 million instruction sentences, VizOIDs appeared in every corpus we examined, including 6.7% of instruction sentences and 35.9% of recipes overall, and 55.5% of recipes in the professionally written Food Network corpus. In a hand-labeled subset, independent human coders reached substantial agreement (κ = 0.730), and an LLM reached near-perfect post-adjudication agreement with human coding (κ = 0.961), showing that the phenomenon is detectable at scale. We then report semi-structured interviews with 12 BLV individuals to examine how they work through these instructions. Participants described a shared repertoire of non-visual cooking knowledge: timing as a proxy, smell, sound, touch, temperature, and familiar utensils used to infer food state. Framed through the social model of disability, our findings show that many recipes are inaccessible because recipe language fails to encode the non-visual knowledge BLV cooks already use. Our findings can inform vision rehabilitation therapists and AI accessibility researchers designing low-cost, language-level interventions that rewrite recipe text at the point of acquisition, grounded in BLV cooks’ lived expertise.

item.title: Prompting Change in the Welfare State: Co-designing an LLM-Assisted Toolkit of Welfare Stories and Tips with Aphasia Communities
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
People with aphasia face substantial barriers when navigating digital welfare systems—including communication impairments, literacy demands and the cognitive burden of bureaucratic processes shaped by decades of austerity. We present Advokit, a multimodal AI toolkit co-designed with people with aphasia to support welfare navigation, application drafting and self-advocacy. Developed through a five-stage participatory design process, Advokit integrates accessible benefit information, a comparative benefits table, lived-experience stories and Benefit Buddy, an LLM-assisted drafting chatbot. Across a three-month real-world deployment, the toolkit recorded 800 visitors and 2,849 page views; users engaged most with the benefits table, benefits list and stories pages—reflecting demand for both structured guidance and peer-grounded narratives. Survey responses (n = 11) were broadly positive, particularly for information access, though Benefit Buddy onboarding scored lower. Analysis of 14 chatbot sessions showed the system excelled at translating established lived experience into application-ready language, but struggled when users first needed orientation before engaging with the drafting workflow. We frame Advokit as counter-infrastructure: a community-built response to the hostile design of the welfare system. Our findings also surface limitations of conversational AI interfaces as access mechanisms: as chatbots are increasingly deployed to mediate access to vital public services. We contribute an open-source co-designed welfare toolkit, empirical findings from its community deployment and design implications for accessible AI-supported public services.

item.title: “What Am I Really Doing with My Own Brain?”: College Students on Learning, Ownership, and AI
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
Generative artificial intelligence gives college students new ways to support their learning, while also raising questions about what they still want to learn and do for themselves. This qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 undergraduates at a Northeastern liberal arts college to examine how students distinguish between AI use that supports their own thinking and AI use that substitutes for it, what they believe is worth doing on their own, and whether and how purpose enters their reasoning about learning and AI use. Using the Framework Method with a cross-case matrix to compare patterns across participants and topics, we found that students repeatedly drew a line between using AI as a supportive tool and letting it take the place of their own thinking or authorship. Students most often talked about wanting to keep developing their own skills, thinking independently, and knowing what they could actually do without AI. They also wanted the work to still feel “like theirs,” citing ownership, pride, authenticity, and ethical concerns. Students also described pressures that made AI appealing, including heavy workloads, deadlines, grades, convenience, and concerns about falling behind their peers. Although few participants explicitly connected their AI choices to a stated purpose, many described concerns that may be relevant to purpose development, including developing valued skills and strengths, acting on personal values, and becoming the kind of person they hoped to be. We consider these concerns through a purpose-mindset framework while distinguishing our interpretation from participants’ own explanations of their AI choices. The findings suggest that understanding students’ AI use requires attention to what they believe they need to learn and do for themselves.

item.title: When college students perceive GAI feedback as credible: the role of perceived GAI feedback credibility in promoting deep learning through cognitive engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has rapidly developed in higher education and has raised new questions from an educational psychology perspective. Why does GAI feedback promote meaningful learning for some college students but fail to produce similar learning benefits for others? To answer this question, this study develops a theoretical framework based on Information Processing Theory, Elaboration Likelihood Model, and Constructivist Learning Theory. This study examines how perceived GAI feedback credibility influences college students’ deep learning and explores the mediating role of cognitive engagement in this relationship. This study adopts a stratified simple sampling method and collects questionnaire data from 506 undergraduate students and uses structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine the proposed model. The results show that perceived GAI feedback credibility has positive relationships with both cognitive engagement and deep learning. In addition, cognitive engagement plays a significant mediating role between perceived GAI feedback credibility and deep learning, suggesting that credible GAI feedback may support deep learning by encouraging college students to engage in cognitive processing and reflective thinking. This study extends research on learning psychology in GAI-supported learning environments by explaining how college students evaluate and process GAI feedback. The findings indicate that the influence of GAI feedback on learning does not simply result from the technology itself. Instead, college students’ judgments of feedback credibility and their following cognitive engagement play important roles in shaping deep learning processes.

item.title: AI literacy is directly associated with positive attitudes and indirectly associated with negative attitudes through AI anxiety: a cross-sectional study of preservice teachers
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Positive and negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) may have partly distinct psychological correlates. This cross-sectional study examined whether AI anxiety statistically accounted for associations between AI literacy and positive and negative attitudes toward AI among preservice teachers. Methods Participants were 335 preservice teachers enrolled in a faculty of education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and a personal information form. Two indirect-effect models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for prior AI training. Results AI literacy was negatively associated with AI anxiety and positively associated with positive attitudes toward AI. AI anxiety was positively associated with negative attitudes but was not significantly associated with positive attitudes. The indirect association through AI anxiety was significant for negative attitudes but not for positive attitudes, and a direct bootstrap contrast confirmed that the two indirect effects differed significantly (B = −0.118, 95% CI [−0.201, −0.039]). Prior AI training was not significantly associated with either attitude dimension. A sensitivity analysis excluding the three reverse-worded AI literacy items reproduced this pattern. Discussion The findings indicate that positive and negative attitudes toward AI may have partly distinct psychological correlates: AI literacy is directly related to positive evaluations, whereas its association with negative evaluations is statistically linked to AI anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional, the indirect effects should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mediation.

item.title: Within-person reciprocal processes between AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement: a three-wave random-intercept cross-lagged panel study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Artificial intelligence (AI) feedback has become a pervasive feature of university learning, yet whether students’ capacity to engage productively with such feedback co-develops with their broader learner agency remains poorly understood. Drawing on student feedback literacy theory, self-determination theory as a supplementary motivational lens, and the mutualism principle, this study tested whether AI feedback literacy and agentic engagement reciprocally predict each other over time at the within-person level and exploratorily examined whether they share a stable trait-level association. A three-wave panel study of 480 Chinese undergraduates ( N = 399 with complete data across all waves), with measurements at six-week intervals across one semester, was analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model (RI-CLPM). At the between-person level, students who scored systematically higher in AI feedback literacy across the semester also scored systematically higher in agentic engagement, with a moderate and statistically significant trait-level correlation between the two random intercepts ( r = 0.315, p < 0.001), supporting Hypothesis 1. At the within-person level, both cross-lagged pathways were positive and significant: deviations in AI feedback literacy predicted later deviations in agentic engagement ( β = 0.222, p < 0.001), and the reverse pathway was likewise significant ( β = 0.263, p < 0.001). A Wald test indicated that the two reciprocal pathways did not differ significantly in magnitude (Δ B = 0.002, p = 0.972), consistent with a symmetric mutualism. A model comparison confirmed that the RI-CLPM provided substantially better fit than a traditional cross-lagged panel model, with the RI-CLPM revealing substantially larger within-person reciprocal effects once stable trait-level covariation was properly isolated. The findings extend the mutualism principle from a coupling of person-internal constructs to a coupling between a person-internal competency and a person-environment behavioral interface. They also raise the possibility, in a Confucian Heritage Culture context where agentic engagement has historically been culturally muted, that AI feedback may offer a less culturally-loaded venue in which students can exercise agency. The study repositions AI feedback literacy from a static skill into a dynamic developmental resource that is constituted, in part, by the very engagement it enables.

item.title: Effects of question-chain prompting on self-regulated learning, metacognition, and achievement in a generative AI environment
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers learners immediate and personalized support, yet unguided interaction may encourage passive use and weaken self-regulated learning (SRL). This study examined whether question-chain prompting can support SRL in human-AI interaction. A quasi-experiment was conducted with 83 undergraduates enrolled in a television program production course. A control group used free-form questioning, whereas two experimental groups used either a progressive or a divergent question-chain strategy. Data included GenAI interaction logs, post-task reflections, metacognitive awareness measures, and course grades. This study found that both question-chain groups demonstrated significantly more learning-strategy and learning-monitoring behaviors than the control group. Reflection data further indicated differences in students’ approaches to human-AI collaboration, although these differences should be interpreted cautiously because the reflection prompts differed by condition. Moreover, both experimental groups scored significantly higher than the control group on knowledge of cognition, regulation of cognition, and academic achievement. No significant differences were found between the progressive and divergent question-chain approaches. The findings suggest that question-chain prompting, implemented as an instructional package of specific, sequenced, and required questions, can promote more active engagement during human-AI interaction and support metacognitive development and learning performance. Question chains offer a practical approach for guiding students’ use of GenAI in educational settings.

item.title: Beyond good and bad: An in-depth study of student and teacher views on generative AI in high school.
item.description:
Technology Mind and Behavior
Public and scholarly discussions of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education often emphasize sharp divides, portraying students as enthusiastic adopters unconcerned with learning and teachers as reluctant gatekeepers focused on control and assessment.However, little empirical work has examined how students' and teachers' attitudes toward AI are formed, expressed, and negotiated in everyday social contexts.We conducted in-depth interviews with 31 high school students and 29 high school teachers from five states in the United States to quantitatively examine how both groups reason about generative AI tools in education.Participants rarely expressed simple endorsement or rejection of AI; instead, they often articulated tensions between perceived benefits and risks.Students and teachers described AI as useful and engaging but also potentially undermining genuine learning and skill development.Participants also expressed uncertainty about appropriate use, the reliability of AI outputs, and the long-term implications of AI for education.Attitudes toward AI were shaped through ongoing peer interaction, with many participants describing how conversations and shared experiences influenced their views.Together, these findings suggest that attitudes toward generative AI in education are best understood as socially negotiated responses to a rapidly evolving technology rather than in terms of generational divides.More broadly, the findings highlight how integrating AI into education requires ongoing reflection about the role technology should play in learning and human development.

item.title: Shaping early childhood in the age of AI: holistic competencies, pedagogical practices, and ecological support
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the learning and developmental contexts in which young children grow, learn, and interact. Guided by an ecological perspective, this systematic conceptual mapping review examines 86 resources to explore what young children should learn and how they should be taught. Four themes were identified through thematic analysis: (1) holistic competencies for young children, encompassing foundational cognitive and social–emotional skills, physical and mental well-being, executive functions, learning dispositions, and AI literacy; (2) governance for AI integration in early childhood education; (3) professional development and systemic support for educators; and (4) play-based learning and human-centered approaches in AI-enhanced contexts. The findings suggest that thriving in the AI age requires moving beyond isolated digital skills toward holistic development, supported by a cohesive infrastructure that links classroom practice with structural governance. These findings highlight the necessity of cultivating holistic competencies beyond basic AI literacy in curriculum design, preparing children to navigate an ever-changing digital world. Furthermore, they underscore the imperative for robust institutional support, particularly through participatory research to support age-appropriate pedagogy and educators’ digital confidence, while highlighting the value of playful early learning. Concurrently, these insights establish a theoretical framework for future empirical research, offer actionable strategies for ethical child-centred AI implementation, and provide strategic directions for policy and practice to address the critical demand for transformative knowledge in early childhood education.

item.title: When AI advice agrees or disagrees with human judgment: trust, self-efficacy, psychological resilience, and adaptive responses in physical education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As AI-based decision-support systems become increasingly embedded in physical education and coaching practice, agreement and disagreement between algorithmic advice and participants’ immediate scenario judgments have become important but theoretically underexamined features of human-AI collaboration. Grounded in a shared Judge-Advisor System paradigm, four scenario-based experiments (total N = 859) manipulated whether an experimentally presented AI recommendation was consistent or conflicting with each participant’s prior judgment and tested machine trust and collaborative decision-making self-efficacy as psychological pathways to self-reported collaborative adaptive responses. Psychological resilience and rationale provision were examined as study-specific boundary conditions. Conflict significantly reduced machine trust (Study 1, d = 1.061) and self-efficacy (Study 2, B = −0.687), and both measured mediators carried significant negative indirect associations with adaptive responses (Study 1, B = −0.428; Study 2, via trust B = −0.201, via self-efficacy B = −0.127). Psychological resilience attenuated the between-condition difference in self-efficacy in Study 3 (index of moderated mediation = 0.115). In Study 4, rationale provision moderated the condition-to-trust association, F (1, 239) = 11.348, p < 0.001, partial η 2 = 0.045: the conflict effect was −0.811 in the black-box condition but −0.182 when a rationale was provided. The manipulation therefore concerns advice-judgment agreement rather than a direct experimental comparison of data-driven judgment with established experiential intuition. Because the scenarios did not establish objective recommendation accuracy, the moderation patterns are interpreted as changes in psychological response rather than as evidence that preserving trust or self-efficacy necessarily improves calibration, decision quality, or welfare.

item.title: Prompt specificity and iterative behaviour in text-to-music co-creation: a secondary analysis of interaction logs and a framework for perceived creative control
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence can lower barriers to musical creation while also shifting consequential decisions away from the user. Methods This study examines that tension through a secondary analysis of the published PAGURI interaction-log prompt corpus and develops a tentative framework for perceived creative control. The analysable corpus contained 304 text-to-music prompts from 24 participants. Musical specificity was operationalised as explicit instrument and technical-parameter markers; iterative continuity was measured with Jaccard similarity between consecutive prompts and checked against TF-IDF cosine similarity. To avoid pseudoreplication, group comparisons were conducted on participant-level summaries rather than treating 304 prompts as independent cases. Results Role-derived experience groups differed substantially in mean prompt specificity, H(2) = 10.25, p = 0.006, ε 2 = 0.39, and specificity density, H(2) = 11.52, p = 0.003, ε 2 = 0.45, but not in refinement rate, H(2) = 0.24, p = 0.888. At a descriptive Jaccard threshold of 0.20, 46.8% of consecutive pairs were refinements and 53.2% were restarts; because this classification was threshold-sensitive, continuous similarity remained the primary continuity measure. Prompt specificity did not increase systematically across the session: the mean within-person Spearman correlation was ρ = −0.06, and the distribution of participant-level correlations did not differ significantly from zero, W = 89.0, p = 0.374. Discussion These findings distinguish the explicit technical-musical information users encode in prompts from the sequential continuity of their prompting behaviour. The paper integrates task structure, system autonomy, model coverage, prior experience, self-efficacy, and psychological ownership into a testable framework for future music-education research. Given the small participant-level sample and role-derived grouping, the empirical findings are exploratory and require confirmation in larger, controlled studies.

item.title: Engagement or disengagement: understanding the emotional dynamics of EFL learners in GenAI-assisted writing from the sociocultural perspective
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has reshaped EFL writing education, yet the emotional dimensions of student engagement in GenAI-assisted writing remain underexplored. This longitudinal multiple-case study investigates how Chinese EFL learners' emotional engagement evolves during a GenAI-assisted college writing course and what factors drive this evolution. Methods Drawing on the sociocultural framework of L2 student engagement with written feedback, we traced the emotional trajectories of three focal students across three writing tasks (exposition, group feature article, and argumentation) within a 14-week course. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews with stimulated recall, reflective reports, GenAI-student chatlogs, drafts, informal chats, and course syllabus, and analyzed via thematic analysis. Results Our findings reveal three qualitatively distinct trajectories: positive-resilient, characterized by sustained positive affect with temporary fluctuations; pragmatic-transformative, marked by a gradual shift from practical disengagement to critical engagement; and vulnerable-contingent, moving from moderate disengagement, through tentative peer-mediated improvement, to eventual breakdown and intensified disengagement. These trajectories were shaped by the dialectical interplay between individual factors (e.g., English proficiency, GenAI literacy, mindsets, beliefs, and emotion regulation) and environmental factors (GenAI-relevant task design, peer and teacher mediation, and institutional policies). Discussion The study extends the sociocultural framework by identifying English proficiency and GenAI literacy as critical developmental competencies, embedding GenAI-related factors across multiple environmental levels, and foregrounding emotional engagement as a dynamic, fluid state that interacts with behavioral and cognitive engagement over time. The findings challenge universalist claims about GenAI's uniform affective benefits and underscore the need for differentiated pedagogical approaches that attend to learners' diverse emotional needs in GenAI-mediated writing contexts.

item.title: GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality in e-commerce: the mediating role of perceived information overload and the moderating role of consumer involvement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to support product search, comparison, and evaluation in e-commerce. However, consumers differ in their ability to use and critically evaluate GenAI-generated information, which may shape their perceived information overload and decision outcomes. Grounded in Information Processing Theory, this study examines the association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality, the mediating role of perceived information overload, and the moderating role of consumer involvement. Data were collected through an online survey of 401 Chinese college students and analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis and bootstrapped mediation and moderation procedures. The results show that GenAI literacy is positively associated with perceived decision quality and negatively associated with perceived information overload. Perceived information overload is negatively associated with perceived decision quality and accounts for a significant indirect association between GenAI literacy and perceived decision quality. Consumer involvement further moderates the association between GenAI literacy and perceived information overload: the negative association is stronger at higher levels of involvement. These findings support an information-processing account in which consumers’ GenAI-related capabilities and motivational involvement jointly shape their perceptions of cognitive burden and decision quality. The study highlights the importance of strengthening consumers’ critical GenAI literacy and adapting AI-supported information presentation to different levels of consumer involvement.

item.title: AI Tutors in Technical Training: Trust, Feedback Timing, and Skill Transfer in Maintenance Tasks
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Technical maintenance training requires learners to develop procedural accuracy, diagnostic reasoning, error recovery, and confidence under realistic conditions. This study examined how AI tutor feedback timing influences trust, over-reliance, and skill transfer in maintenance tasks. Participants completed procedures under three conditions: immediate feedback, delayed feedback, and adaptive feedback triggered by hesitation, repeated errors, or safety-critical risk. Outcomes included training accuracy, recovery quality, completion time, cognitive workload, tutor trust, feedback acceptance, and unaided transfer performance. Immediate feedback improved early accuracy and reduced procedural errors but increased step-by-step dependence and weakened independent troubleshooting. Delayed feedback produced mixed effects, supporting autonomy for some learners while increasing frustration and avoidable mistakes for others. Adaptive feedback produced the strongest results by allowing independent attempts while intervening when support was needed. It improved unaided transfer, error recovery, procedural sequencing, and trust calibration. Overall, AI tutors were most effective when feedback scaffolded learning without replacing trainee judgment.

item.title: Do You Feel Like Using GenAI? Scenario Emotional Valence Impact on Potential Generative Artificial Intelligence Use
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) is becoming increasingly ubiquitous, creating questions about what factors are influencing its use. This study explored whether emotions in decision-making scenarios impact the use of genAI writing tools. We presented 35 writing-based scenarios, some associated with the six basic human emotions (sadness, anger, enjoyment, fear, surprise, disgust) and others created as neutral emotional conditions. College student participants were asked whether they would use a genAI tool to complete the task, and then to identify the emotion present. Most participants varied their decision to use AI tools. There were significant effects of emotion on the potential use of genAI assistance, with a higher intended adoption for fear and surprise contexts. Emotion strength also influenced potential AI use, with reported AI trust and task complexity increasing in stronger-rated scenarios. However, the overall rate of AI use was generally low. Implications for automation use and trust theories are discussed.

item.title: Between automation and epistemic autonomy: reappropriating generative AI in global academic writing
item.description:
Learning Media and Technology
This article examines the epistemic implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic writing within unequal knowledge infrastructures. I conceptualize it as an epistemic apparatus: a sociotechnical arrangement that mediates credibility, voice, and scholarly legitimacy. Drawing on epistemic injustice theory, post- and decolonial scholarship, and critical AI studies, the article argues that GenAI can reinforce dominant Anglophone norms of academic form, reshaping the conditions under which knowledge becomes legible and publishable. I argue that these effects emerge through interactions among models, writing practices, and institutional expectations. Through two author-constructed fictional analytic vignettes, the article illustrates how selective uptake, compromise, diagnostic testing, and refusal can operate as practices of judgment within AI-mediated writing. I conceptualize epistemic autonomy as situated authority over scholarly judgment and advance critical epistemic literacy as a pedagogical orientation for exercising that authority under algorithmic mediation. The article concludes by proposing an epistemic ethics of governance oriented toward traceability, plurality, infrastructural accountability, and the protection of bounded use and refusal.

item.title: When AI Enters the Pencil Box: A Longitudinal Study of Child–LLM Writing Collaboration in a Chinese Primary School
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
We report a qualitative study spanning more than six months with upper-primary students (ages 9–12) in southern China using a local LLM (Doubao) for writing. Two interview waves with ten students (nine re-interviewed) and six teachers (three re-interviewed) reveal a set of recurring shifts in our focal cohort: from novelty to strategy, from anthropomorphic “companion/virtual teacher” to tool-like framing, and from quick unsticking to guarded use shaped by dependence, fairness, and exam-transfer Footnote1 concerns. Students valued speed and breadth but noted mechanical tone, age/style mismatch, and weak transfer to AI-free tests. We map a Control × Dependency framework and before/after transitions, and surface tensions around classroom norms and equity amid policy ambiguity and uneven AI literacy. We suggest process-visible, agency-preserving integration: sentence- and phrase-level provenance with mandatory micro-edits, task-specific scaffold ceilingsFootnote2, and process-anchored assessment schemes that explicitly factor in AI-use traces.

item.title: Data science for K-12: A design-based research study
item.description:
Educational Technology Research and Development
Abstract Data science is a field that merges advancements in computer science, statistics, and machine learning. To date, much data science instruction has been through graduate programs or self-directed course offerings. There are therefore fewer opportunities for formal data science education, especially for K-12 educators and learners who have limited exposure to these fields. While some efforts have emerged to introduce data science in pre-college settings, there is little research regarding learning design strategies that support data science for inservice teachers. As such, this project employs a design-based research (DBR) approach to develop accessible and engaging open-access learning resources as a way to reduce barriers to data science instruction across the educational spectrum. Given the gap regarding data science in K-12, our DBR study identifies the following design elements: (a) revised data science content scope, (b) design standardization for interactive learning, (c) reframing data science for case-based learning, (d) artificial intelligence (AI) towards data personalization, and (e) data science coding through goal-based learning. The project also introduces aspects of the curriculum via a teacher professional development, which provides important insights and challenges regarding data science at the middle and high school levels. Implications for learning design, open-educational resources, data science standards, and others are discussed.

item.title: Human-Centered AI Metacognition: Development and Validation of a Scale for Preserving Cognitive Autonomy in Human–AI Collaboration
item.description:
Journal of Intelligence
The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming human cognitive activities and creating a growing need to preserve cognitive autonomy in human–AI interactions. Although recent research has examined metacognition in AI-mediated environments, existing work has primarily focused on improving AI use and human–AI collaboration, with less attention to how individuals regulate the role and extent of AI involvement in their own cognitive activities. To address this gap, the present study introduced Human-Centered AI Metacognition (HC-AIM), defined as the capacity to recognize AI capabilities and limitations, monitor AI-generated information, and regulate the extent to which AI participates in one’s own cognitive activities while maintaining cognitive autonomy. Across three studies, we developed the Chinese version of the Human-Centered AI Metacognition Scale (HC-AIMS) and conducted an initial psychometric evaluation. Study 1 examined the scale structure using exploratory factor analysis and supported a predominantly unidimensional structure with good internal consistency. Study 2 examined this structure using confirmatory factor analysis and provided evidence of its convergent validity through its association with general metacognition. Study 3 further replicated the scale structure and internal consistency and examined its relationships with AI literacy, collaborative AI metacognition, and autonomous cognitive offloading. HC-AIM was positively associated with all three constructs. Comparisons of theoretically specified factor models provided preliminary evidence of empirical distinguishability between HC-AIM and both AI literacy and collaborative AI metacognition, despite substantial correlations with these constructs. HC-AIM was also positively associated with autonomous cognitive offloading, providing complementary self-reported criterion-related evidence for its validity. Taken together, the findings suggest that HC-AIM represents a contextualized, human-centered form of metacognitive regulation that is closely related to broader metacognitive and AI-related competencies while specifically emphasizing the regulation of AI participation in human cognition. The Chinese version of the HC-AIMS provides a theoretically grounded starting point for investigating human cognition and cognitive autonomy in AI-mediated environments.

item.title: From AI labels to trust: cognitive pathways linking authenticity judgments, risk perception, and trust in AI-generated videos
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) has raised concerns regarding the authenticity and trustworthiness of synthetic media. Although AI disclosure labels are increasingly used as transparency mechanisms, the cognitive processes through which these cues influence trust formation remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to develop and test a cognitive pathway model explaining how AI disclosure labels, authenticity judgments, perceived risk, cognitive processing styles, and literacy factors shape trust toward AI-generated videos. Methods A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 617 participants randomly assigned to four conditions involving AI-generated instructional videos with different AI label and video quality combinations. Participants evaluated authenticity, systematic and heuristic processing, trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, sharing intention, AI literacy, and media literacy. Regression, bootstrapped mediation, and moderation analyses were performed. Results AI disclosure labels significantly reduced perceived authenticity but did not directly affect trust, adoption, sharing intention, or perceived risk. Trust formation occurred through cognitive pathways: systematic processing increased trust, whereas heuristic processing reduced trust. Authenticity enhanced trust and lowered perceived risk, with perceived risk mediating the authenticity–trust relationship. Trust positively predicted adoption and sharing intentions, while AI and media literacy moderated selected relationships. Conclusion Trust in AI-generated videos was not directly determined by transparency labels alone. Instead, the observed associations among authenticity judgments, perceived risk, information processing, and trust were consistent with a multi-stage cognitive interpretation, although the cross-sectional post-exposure measurement of these constructs does not establish their temporal or causal sequence.

item.title: Generative artificial intelligence use and interpersonal educational interaction among nursing students: self-regulated learning as a statistical mediator
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is reshaping health sciences education. For nursing students, educational interaction (EI), self-regulated learning (SRL), and GAI interaction are all particularly important. However, these relationships and their processes remain underexplored. Methods A total of 1020 nursing students were recruited from one medical university in Hunan Province in China. The Demographics Questionnaire, the Chinese version of Student-GAI interaction scale, the Educational Interaction Scale, and the Self-regulated Learning Questionnaire were administered. SPSS 22.0 and AMOS 24.0 software were used to analyze the data. Results The mean scores of student-GAI interaction (SGI) and EI were 14.80 ± 2.27 and 70.90 ± 8.15, respectively. Significant positive relationships were found among all three variables (all P < 0.01). Both SGI (β = 0.256) and SRL (β = 0.520) positively were associated with EI (both P < 0.001). Furthermore, SGI showed a significant direct association with EI, with a direct effect value of 0.92 ( P < 0.001). SRL statistically mediated the association between SGI and EI, with a significant indirect effect value of 0.44. The mediating effect represented 32.35% of the total effect ( P < 0.001). Dimension-specific analyses revealed that the mediating effect was strongest for student-teacher interaction (45.41%) and student-content interaction (41.54%). Conclusions SGI is positively associated with EI among nursing students, both directly and indirectly through SRL. Educational strategies that encourage effective GAI use and strengthen SRL may be associated with enhanced EI in nursing education.

item.title: Generative AI as a team moderator in CSCL : Facilitating students' multidimensional engagement through adaptive scaffolding for socially shared regulation of learning
item.description:
British Journal of Educational Technology
Abstract Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is essential for successful collaboration, yet effectively scaffolding it remains challenging because regulatory needs are dynamic and context‐dependent. While generative AI (GenAI) offers potential for adaptive support, current applications in collaborative learning largely position it as a content‐oriented tutor for knowledge explanation or idea generation, leaving its role as a process‐oriented team moderator for scaffolding SSRL processes underexplored. To address this gap, we conducted a 16‐week quasi‐experiment with 64 undergraduates in China, comparing adaptive SSRL scaffolding delivered by a GenAI agent in the adaptive‐SSRL condition with static scaffolding via structured digital worksheets in the static‐SSRL condition. Survey data and group discussion transcripts were analysed using statistical methods and epistemic network analysis. Results indicated several differences in students' multidimensional engagement between the two conditions: (1) Behaviourally, the adaptive‐SSRL group showed significantly higher participation equality, although participation intensity did not differ significantly between groups. (2) Cognitively, the adaptive‐SSRL group demonstrated deeper cognitive engagement, reflected in more advanced cognitive presence phases and more integrative, solution‐oriented discourse patterns. (3) Emotionally, the adaptive‐SSRL group reported significantly higher overall emotional engagement, particularly feeling more relaxed during collaboration and more connected with peers. These findings extend human–AI collaboration research by showing that GenAI can function as an SSRL‐informed team moderator rather than a content‐oriented tutor. They also offer design implications for GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding and human–AI role division in CSCL. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) is critical for successful collaboration and is closely associated with the quality of student engagement. While static scaffolds (eg, worksheets) provide a basic regulatory structure, they fail to adapt to the dynamic and emergent needs of collaborating teams. Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly used for personalised content support, yet its potential as a process‐oriented team moderator remains underexplored. What this paper adds This study introduced SSRLAgent, a GenAI agent grounded in SSRL theory and established principles of collective metacognitive support, to provide adaptive and interactive regulatory scaffolding. In a 16‐week quasi‐experiment, we compared GenAI‐enabled adaptive SSRL scaffolding (SSRLAgent) with static scaffolding (structured digital worksheets) in CSCL. Adaptive‐SSRL scaffolding was associated with higher‐quality engagement: greater participation equality, deeper cognitive engagement and higher overall emotional engagement. Implications for practice and/or policy The study underscores the necessity of shifting SSRL scaffolding from static, ‘one‐size‐fits‐all’ support to adaptive GenAI interventions to improve collaborative engagement. The findings provide design guidance for developing SSRL agents that are embedded in the shared interaction space and responsive to groups' moment‐to‐moment regulatory needs. The study suggests a productive human–AI division of labour: GenAI agents can support process coordination and regulatory prompting, while teachers and peers remain essential for relationally complex forms of support that collaborative learning requires.

item.title: Mathematics teachers’ AI-TMPK: exploring structural relationships and latent profiles
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
With the rapid integration of AI into mathematics education, mathematics teachers’ professional knowledge requires reconstruction. This study proposed an artificial intelligence–technological mathematical pedagogical knowledge (AI-TMPK) framework for primary and secondary mathematics teachers and developed a corresponding scale. The results showed that the AI-TMPK scale comprised 8 dimensions and 36 items, demonstrating satisfactory validity, reliability, and measurement invariance across gender and school level. XK indirectly affected AI-TMPK through AI-TK, AI-TMK, and AI-TPK, while AI-TK played a central role in transforming MK and PK into AI-integrated knowledge. AI-TPK and AI-TMK significantly predicted AI-TMPK, and AI-related knowledge showed stronger explanatory power than traditional knowledge domains. Latent profile analysis identified three teacher groups: imbalanced-weak, balanced-development, and mature-integration, with the mature-integration type being the largest. Teachers performed better in traditional non-technical knowledge than in technology-related knowledge. Gender significantly predicted profile membership, whereas school level did not. The AI-TMPK framework and scale enrich the theory of mathematics teachers’ professional knowledge in the AI era and inform assessment, differentiated training, and educational support.

item.title: From growth mindset to social-emotional skills in early and mid-adolescence: A educational-cultural examination of an integrated mind-body-behavior framework
item.description:
Learning and Instruction
Background Social-emotional learning (SEL) is a core educational goal, yet little is known about how adolescents’ cognitive beliefs, body-related self-perceptions, and everyday health behavior jointly relate to social-emotional skills across diverse cultural contexts and school stages. Objective Based on mindset theory and self-regulation perspectives, we examined an integrated Mind-Body-Behavior framework in which growth mindset, positive body image, and health behavior show a theoretically specified pattern of associated with adolescents’ social-emotional skills. Sample Participants were 62,105 adolescents from 15 regions where data were drawn from the OECD 2023 Study on Social and Emotional Skills. Methods A two-stage quantitative design combined structural equation modeling and machine learning. Results Growth mindset was associated with social-emotional skills both directly and indirectly associations via body image and health behavior. The direct association was substantially stronger than the combined indirect associations, indicating partial rather than complete support for the full proposed pattern. Scalar invariance across the seven clusters was not supported, so cluster-level comparisons were treated as descriptive. Associations differed between cohorts: the association between growth mindset and body image was stronger in the younger cohort, whereas the association between health behavior and social-emotional skills was stronger in the older cohort. Conclusions The study contributes an integrated view of how beliefs, body-related self-perception, and health behavior relate to social-emotional skills. The framework shows that cognitive, body-related, and behavioral domains each relate to adolescents’ social-emotional skills and that these relations change between school stages.

item.title: Patterns of morphology in children’s print: estimates of polymorphemic vocabulary using an innovative, AI-informed database of British and American word families
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Morphological complexity is a pervasive feature of the vocabulary children encounter in print, yet resources for investigating morphology remain limited. What morpheme patterns do children encounter in print? Which morphemes cover how many polymorphic words in reading experiences? In this study we introduce the British and American Word Families (BAWF) project, an innovative open database of ∼378,000 words, and use it to address questions such as these. Methods GPT-4.1 was fine-tuned using ∼6000 morphologically-coded words from an existing human-generated database (Morpholex). The fine-tuned LLM coded word-parts in all Wiktionary words attested in large British and American corpora. Performance was evaluated via agreement with existing databases. Classical roots were attributed to a subset of words by mapping a list of roots from Wikipedia to all related entries in Wiktionary. The resulting BAWF database is then used to estimate morpheme patterns across databases of children’s texts and further developed as an online application. Results LLM word part predictions are good and fall within the range of agreement typical of existing databases. Nonetheless, output contains some error/noise. In children’s print, polymorphemic words increase across picturebooks to juvenile fiction and school-reading programs. Greek-Latin root words occur early and commonly. Estimates include that ∼100 prefixes/suffixes may account for nearly all derivations. The BAWF itself is released open-source https://cgg-projects.github.io/BAWF_V1/ , with many lexical, morphological, and psycholinguistic variables, including but not limited to frequency, family size, and morpheme-counts. Discussion The contribution suggests that instruction that prioritizes high-yield morphemes could give children access to large word families. These morphemes are present and common early in print. The BAWF (V1) helps see which may be useful to teach. Users can generate custom wordlists, targeting particular features and families, and access linked dictionary/etymological information. The platform includes AI-assisted searches, explanations, parsing review/corrections, and instructional support. The BAWF project will develop over time, incorporating additional variables (e.g., morphological transparency), improving accuracy and the user interface.

item.title: AI feedback does not motivate by itself: a motivational-meaning model for university physical education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.

item.title: Technology‐Supported Formative Assessment in Higher Education: AI , Learning Analytics and the Future of Assessment for Learning
item.description:
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
ABSTRACT Purpose This study examines the intellectual and thematic development of technology‐supported formative assessment (TSFA) in higher education and its convergence with feedback, learning analytics, artificial intelligence (AI) and self‐regulation. Design/Methodology/Approach A scoping review integrating bibliometric mapping, qualitative thematic synthesis and SWOT analysis was conducted on TSFA literature published between 2000 and 2026 (August). Findings The findings reveal accelerated growth after 2020 and a shift from technology‐centred applications towards learner‐centred, adaptive and data‐informed formative assessment. However, theoretical fragmentation, limited longitudinal evidence, ethical concerns and geographical inequalities remain. Originality/Value The study conceptualises TSFA as a technology‐mediated formative ecosystem integrating technological capacity, pedagogical regulation, learner agency and human judgement. Practical Implications Institutions should prioritise human‐centred AI integration, transparent governance, equitable access and professional development to ensure that technology supports rather than replaces formative pedagogical judgement.

item.title: Prompt‐based emotional scaffolding in generative AI : Effects on self‐regulated learning and socio‐emotional outcomes
item.description:
British Journal of Educational Technology
Abstract While generative AI (GenAI) tools are emerging as educational resources, general‐purpose applications like ChatGPT are not explicitly designed to support the metacognitive and socio‐emotional dimensions of learning, often failing to address students' emotional states or promote independent thinking. In response, this study introduces a CVT‐SRL GenAI Support Framework integrating control‐value theory (CVT) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) and tests a learner‐centred GenAI chatbot design employing prompt‐based SRL scaffolding and emotional support. In a preregistered experiment in an authentic educational setting, 144 high school students were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: (1) ChatGPT, (2) SRLbot (GenAI with SRL scaffolding), (3) emotional SRLbot (GenAI with SRL and emotional support). Outcomes included conceptual knowledge and transfer, trace‐based and self‐reported engagement in SRL phases (forethought, performance, self‐reflection), enjoyment, boredom, hopelessness, self‐efficacy and trust. Data were collected at pretest, posttest and 4‐week follow‐up. Across conditions, students showed improvements in conceptual knowledge and transfer from pretest to posttest, with no significant condition differences in post‐to‐follow‐up change. Both SRLbot and Emotional SRLbot were associated with higher self‐reported enjoyment and lower boredom than ChatGPT and elicited trace‐based SRL behaviours. Moreover, Emotional SRLbot prompted greater engagement in performance‐phase and self‐reflection processes than the other conditions. These findings provide preliminary evidence that GenAI agents integrating SRL and emotional scaffolding can support more positive emotional states and task‐level SRL behaviours than general‐purpose GenAI, highlighting control‐value appraisals as a promising target for emotionally supportive SRL design. Future research should explore longitudinal effects on SRL skill development and independent regulation. Practitioner notes What is already known about this topic Generative AI (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT have shown promise in enhancing learning outcomes, but they also present challenges in supporting socio‐emotional needs, fostering metacognition and promoting higher‐order thinking. Applying self‐regulated learning (SRL) frameworks in chatbot‐assisted learning has been found to foster learner autonomy, long‐term engagement and improved learning outcomes. Achievement emotions experienced during learning play a critical role in supporting self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic achievement. Interventions that target learners' perceptions of control and value through reappraisal can effectively foster positive emotions. What this paper adds An investigation of the impact of three GenAI conversational agents (standard ChatGPT, an SRL agent and an emotionally supportive SRL agent) on cognitive and socio‐emotional outcomes as well as task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours among high school students in an authentic classroom setting. Preliminary evidence that integrating prompts which target self‐regulated learning phases and learners' emotional states, as well as address perceptions of control and value can increase students' enjoyment of concrete learning situations and reduce boredom more effectively than standard ChatGPT. Insights into how theoretically grounded GenAI agents that incorporate SRL and emotional scaffolding may support students' emotional engagement and task‐level self‐regulatory behaviours during a short classroom learning activity. Implications for practice and/or policy Prompt engineering can be used to simulate emotional support and personalize guidance based on SRL and emotion regulation principles, providing design considerations for future learner‐centred GenAI systems. Developers and educators aiming to design pedagogically meaningful GenAI tools should focus on scaffolding SRL both cognitively and emotionally, to support the affective and self‐regulatory dimensions of learning. We make the technical specifications and system prompts publicly available.
